summary.case_overview: Writ Petition (Civil) No. 135 of 1970 was instituted by Kesavananda Bharati against the State of Kerala under Article 32 of the Constitution of India to challenge the constitutional validity of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended [Page 1]. During the pendency of the proceedings, additional state enactments were passed and the Constitution (Twenty-fourth, Twenty-fifth, and Twenty-ninth Amendment) Acts were enacted, leading to amendments in the writ petition to challenge these constitutional amendments [Page 1] [Page 2]. The case was referred to a 13-Judge Bench to determine the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 and to re-examine the correctness of the Supreme Court's earlier decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab [Page 1] [Page 2]. The judgment addresses the relationship between Fundamental Rights under Part III, Directive Principles of State Policy under Part IV, and the scope of constituent power under Article 368 [Page 2] [Page 18] [Page 19] [Page 485].
summary.facts_of_case: The petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 on March 21, 1970 under Article 32 of the Constitution, seeking enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31, and praying that the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 be declared unconstitutional and void [Page 1]. Rule nisi was issued on March 25, 1970 [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 was enacted and received Presidential assent on August 7, 1971, following which the petitioner sought permission to challenge this Act [Page 1]. In April 1971, the Supreme Court in Kunjukutty Sahib v. State of Kerala upheld a High Court decision striking down certain provisions of the Kerala land reform legislation [Page 1] [Page 2]. Thereafter, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act on November 5, 1971, the Twenty-fifth Amendment Act on April 20, 1972, and the Twenty-ninth Amendment Act on June 9, 1972 [Page 2]. The Twenty-ninth Amendment inserted the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Acts of 1969 and 1971 into the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution as Entries 65 and 66 [Page 2]. The Supreme Court granted leave to amend the writ petition to challenge these constitutional amendments, issued notices to the Advocates-General, and referred the matter to a 13-Judge Bench to decide the scope of Article 368 and whether Golak Nath was correctly decided [Page 1] [Page 2].
summary.legal_issues:
The major constitutional questions evaluated in the judgment include:
1. What is the extent and scope of the power conferred on Parliament to amend the Constitution under Article 368, and whether that power enables Parliament to abrogate or abridge fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 78]?
2. Was I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab correctly decided in holding that a constitutional amendment under Article 368 is 'law' within the prohibition of Article 13(2) [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 485]?
3. Are there inherent or implied limitations on the amending power under Article 368 that restrict Parliament from altering or damaging the basic structure, essential features, or identity of the Constitution [Page 6] [Page 91] [Page 104] [Page 258]?
4. What is the constitutional validity of the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 [Page 1] [Page 129] [Page 494]?
5. What is the constitutional validity of Section 2 and Section 3 (introducing Article 31C) of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1972 [Page 1] [Page 194] [Page 361] [Page 495] [Page 498]?
6. What is the constitutional validity of the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 500]?
summary.important_arguments_or_content:
Arguments by the Petitioners:
- The petitioners argued that Parliament's power under Article 368 is limited and does not extend to abrogating or destroying the basic structure, essential features, or identity of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 91] [Page 2177].
- They submitted that fundamental rights are natural, primordial, and inalienable freedoms meant to protect citizens from future tyranny [Page 2] [Page 181] [Page 2177].
- They contended that Article 31C subverts core constitutional features, removes judicial review through conclusive declarations, and enables ordinary legislatures to bypass the formal amendment procedure of Article 368 [Page 2] [Page 245] [Page 496].

Arguments by the Respondents:
- The respondents submitted that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is plenary, unrestricted, and sui generis, enabling it to amend any provision of the Constitution, including Part III rights [Page 2] [Page 7] [Page 104].
- They claimed that short of total repeal of the Constitution, Parliament can alter any feature of Government to implement the Directive Principles of State Policy, particularly Article 39(b) and (c) [Page 2] [Page 104] [Page 194] [Page 284].
- They submitted that no inherent or implied limitations exist in Article 368, and that a constitutional amendment is not ordinary 'law' within the scope of Article 13(2) [Page 6] [Page 104] [Page 485].
summary.court_reasoning:
1. Rejection of Golak Nath and Source of Amending Power: The Court reasoned that Article 368 contains both the power and procedure for constitutional amendments, and that the amending power is not derived from residuary legislative powers under Article 248 or Entry 97 of List I [Page 129] [Page 155] [Page 309] [Page 501]. An amendment passed under Article 368 is an exercise of constituent power, distinct from ordinary legislative law under Articles 107–111 and 245, and is therefore not 'law' subject to Article 13(2) [Page 117] [Page 485] [Page 486] [Page 501].

2. Basic Structure and Amending Power: Judges including Sikri C.J., Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, Jaganmohan Reddy, and Khanna JJ. reasoned that while Article 368 confers broad power to amend every article, 'amendment' does not mean total repeal or destruction, and Parliament cannot alter the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution [Page 8] [Page 258] [Page 309] [Page 374]. Other judges (Ray, Palekar, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, and Chandrachud JJ.) reasoned that Article 368 is plenary and contains no implied or inherent limitations restricting the scope of constitutional change [Page 181] [Page 296] [Page 501].

3. Twenty-fourth Amendment: The Court reasoned that the 24th Amendment is valid as it merely clarified the pre-existing legal position that Parliament exercises constituent power under Article 368 and that Article 13 does not apply to constitutional amendments [Page 129] [Page 374] [Page 494] [Page 501].

4. Twenty-fifth Amendment (Section 2 - Article 31(2)): Replacing 'compensation' with 'amount' means the legislature is no longer bound to provide market value or 'just equivalent', but the amount fixed or principles laid down cannot be illusory or arbitrary [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 374] [Page 497] [Page 498].

5. Twenty-fifth Amendment (Section 3 - Article 31C): The Court reasoned that while protecting laws enacted to secure Article 39(b) and (c) from Articles 14, 19, and 31 is permissible, the second part of Article 31C barring judicial review through a conclusive declaration ('and no law containing a declaration...') excludes judicial scrutiny and exceeds the amending power under Article 368 [Page 374] [Page 258] [Page 501] [Page 502]. Courts retain jurisdiction to examine if a direct and reasonable nexus exists between the law and Article 39(b) or (c) [Page 425] [Page 500] [Page 501] [Page 502].

6. Twenty-ninth Amendment: Placing the Kerala acts into the Ninth Schedule is valid under Article 31B [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 501].
summary.decision_or_conclusion:
The Court held as follows:
1. The decision of the majority in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab is incorrect; Article 368 contains both power and procedure to amend the Constitution, and a constitutional amendment is not 'law' within Article 13(2) [Page 129] [Page 309] [Page 374] [Page 501].
2. The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 is valid [Page 129] [Page 374] [Page 494] [Page 501].
3. Section 2 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1972 is valid [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501].
4. Section 3 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1972 (introducing Article 31C) is valid in respect of its first part, but the second part barring judicial review ('and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court...') is unconstitutional and invalid / severed [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501] [Page 502].
5. The Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 is valid [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 501].
6. The writ petitions were remitted to a Constitution Bench for determination of their validity in accordance with law [Page 374] [Page 502].

summary.simplified_explanation: In this case, the Supreme Court evaluated whether Parliament has unlimited power to alter any part of the Indian Constitution, including fundamental rights like property, equality, and freedom [Page 2]. The Court overruled its earlier Golak Nath judgment, ruling that amending the Constitution is an exercise of constituent power, not ordinary legislative lawmaking, so fundamental rights do not automatically block constitutional amendments under Article 13(2) [Page 129] [Page 309] [Page 485]. However, the Court established that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is not unlimited and cannot be used to destroy or alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 258] [Page 374]. The Court upheld the 24th and 29th Amendments and Section 2 of the 25th Amendment [Page 258] [Page 374]. Regarding Article 31C (Section 3 of the 25th Amendment), the Court held that while Parliament can protect laws giving effect to socio-economic goals under Article 39(b) and (c), it cannot take away the power of courts to review whether a law actually has a real nexus to those goals [Page 374] [Page 258] [Page 501] [Page 502].
